title: Indian American Officials to Hold Capitol Hill Roundtable on Rising Hate Crimes
excerpt: Indian American Impact is convening lawmakers and South Asian elected officials on September 2 to address a surge in hate targeting the community.
body:
• Indian American Impact is convening a roundtable on Capitol Hill on September 2, bringing together Indian American members of Congress and state and local officials
  • 48% of South Asian adults in the U.S. experienced race-based harassment in 2024, according to Stop AAPI Hate data
  • Recent incidents include an Indian flag torn at a Texas rally, calls to deport "every Indian" by a Florida official, and the beheading of an Indian American man in Dallas
  • The roundtable will announce commitments and next steps to combat anti-South Asian discrimination

Indian American Impact, an advocacy organization, is convening a roundtable on Capitol Hill on September 2, bringing together Indian American members of Congress alongside state and local South Asian elected officials to address what it describes as a surge in hate and discrimination targeting South Asian American communities.

The Scale of the Problem

South Asian Americans are experiencing a dramatic rise in hate incidents, according to Indian American Impact, citing Stop AAPI Hate data showing that 48 percent of South Asian adults in the United States experienced race-based harassment in 2024. The organization contends that number has only grown as anti-immigrant rhetoric has escalated from online spaces into mainstream politics.

https://x.com/IndianVCA/status/2094310872256753677

The roundtable comes after a series of high-profile incidents that have alarmed the community. On June 3, 2026, a man tore an Indian flag outside Frisco, Texas City Hall while chanting anti-India slogans at a far-right anti-immigration rally. A Florida city council member called for the deportation of "every Indian" and later called Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi a "foreign occupier." An Arizona state representative called for Rep. Pramila Jayapal to be "tried, convicted, and hanged." In Dallas, an Indian American man was beheaded, and users in extremist online spaces called him an "H-1B scammer."

Congressional Action

Indian American members of Congress, informally known as the "Samosa Caucus," have been pushing for stronger federal action. Earlier this year, Representatives Krishnamoorthi, Ro Khanna, Ami Bera, Pramila Jayapal and Shri Thanedar jointly requested a briefing from the Department of Justice on its strategy for combating anti-Hindu hate crimes, following a series of temple vandalism incidents across the country.

"Attacks at mandirs from New York to California have contributed to increased collective anxiety among Hindu Americans. Our communities remain concerned about law enforcement coordination regarding these bias-motivated crimes."

— Joint letter from five Indian American members of Congress

The Justice Department subsequently reaffirmed its commitment to expanding outreach to the Hindu American community, though Krishnamoorthi noted that "significant challenges remain."

Broader Context

The roundtable follows Hindu Advocacy Day on Capitol Hill in July, which drew bipartisan support from congressional representatives. That event highlighted research showing that what was reported as "anti-Indian" sentiment was often specifically targeted at Hindus, their festivals and their temples, fueled by geopolitics and amplified by online networks.

What to Watch

The September 2 convening will be followed by a press availability where participants and Impact leadership will announce specific commitments and policy next steps. For Indian Americans, the outcome could signal whether federal and state officials are prepared to treat anti-South Asian hate as a distinct and growing civil rights concern.
